content:
An NGO that is offered goods every week should put one in-kind donations page on its website that says what it accepts today, what it cannot accept and why, where and when to drop items off, how to request a pickup, and what paperwork the donor will receive. Behind it sit a needs list staff can edit from a phone, a pickup form with area and quantity rules, and an admin log that turns each offer into a tracked record. In NGO website development in India this page is usually missing: goods are handled through calls to a trustee's mobile and WhatsApp photos of old sofas, while the website talks only about money. The honest part matters as much as the convenient part. Under Indian income-tax law a donor's deduction is available only for a donation of a sum of money, so the page must never promise an 80G receipt for clothes, grain or furniture.

## Why a page beats phone calls and WhatsApp photos

- **It filters before anyone picks up the phone.** A donor who reads "we cannot take used mattresses or opened medicines" does not call about them.
- **It steers people towards what is short.** Many will buy 5 kg of dal instead of clearing a cupboard, if told dal is what the kitchen needs.
- **It stops unusable goods at the gate.** Published condition standards shrink the pile of torn clothing and broken toys someone has to dispose of.
- **It creates a record** with a date, a name, an item list and a status.
- **It is found in search** by people looking for where to donate clothes, books or food in their city.

## What the in-kind donations page must say

### What you accept, what you cannot, and why

List both, and give the reason for each refusal. The table is an example for a children's shelter; yours will differ.

| Item | Position | Reason shown on the page |
|---|---|---|
| Dry rations in sealed packs | Accepted | At least three months before expiry |
| Children's clothes, washed | Accepted | No tears or stains; sorted by age if possible |
| Cooked food | By prior arrangement | We need quantity, cooking time and transport details first |
| Used mattresses, soft toys | Not accepted | We cannot clean them safely |
| Medicines | Not accepted | We have no pharmacist to check and store them |
| Large furniture, electronics | Ask first | Limited storage; working items only; send a photo |

Two categories need extra care.

**Food.** FSSAI framed the Food Safety and Standards (Recovery and Distribution of Surplus Food) Regulations, 2019 to, in its words, protect organisations and individuals who donate food in good faith and to encourage donation to non-profits. Published summaries say the regulations took effect on Gazette publication on 26 July 2019, require surplus food to be distributed before expiry or while fit for consumption, require unfit food to be kept apart in a container marked "Food for Disposal", require food handlers to be trained in hygiene, and prescribe records such as donor name and address, date, product, batch, expiry date, quantity and temperature. If you collect surplus food from restaurants or caterers, confirm with FSSAI or a food-safety adviser what registration and records apply to you. On the website, a food offer form must capture what the food is, when it was cooked or its expiry date, storage and quantity.

**Medicines.** We found no primary source we could cite on what a charity may accept from the public, so we state no rule. The safe wording is that you do not accept medicines from individuals, and that institutional offers go only through your medical team or a registered pharmacist. Confirm the legal position with a qualified adviser.

### Condition standards and a dated needs list

"Gently used" means nothing. Write the gate test: washed, no tears, zips working, shoes in pairs, books with all pages, toys with all parts, appliances that switch on. Add photographs of both kinds. Next to the needs list show "Updated 14 November 2026", generated by the system and not typed by hand, because an undated list is assumed to be stale.

## The live wish list: how to structure it in the CMS

The wish list changes weekly, so it must be a content type staff can edit without a developer. Each item needs:

- item name and a one-line specification ("Toor dal, sealed 1 kg or 5 kg packs");
- category and the programme or centre it is for;
- an urgency flag (urgent, needed, enough for now), or quantity needed against quantity received;
- whether it must be new or can be used;
- a "needed by" date for seasonal items;
- a visible or hidden switch.

Give editing rights to the person who knows the storeroom, and make the edit screen work on a phone. Show "enough for now" items greyed out ("Notebooks: enough until March"), which prevents another fifty arriving and proves the list is real. Leave rupee values off the items, and offer a link to your donation page beside each category for people who would sooner fund the purchase.

### Buy-and-ship wish lists

Some NGOs keep a wish list on an online marketplace so donors can order items for delivery. State it neutrally: name the marketplace, say the purchase is between the donor and the seller, and that the order invoice is not a donation receipt from you. Ask donors to tell you an order is coming, or parcels arrive with no name to thank. Check the marketplace's own terms first.

## Drop-off points with hours and a map

For each point publish the full address with a landmark and a map link that opens directions; days and hours, including the lunch break; who to ask for and a number answered during those hours; notes on parking and the largest item you can receive; and what happens on arrival.

Store drop-off points as structured entries so one edit updates the page, the pickup form and the confirmation message. Keep the same hours on your Google Business Profile, and give temporary collection points an end date so they disappear automatically.

## The pickup request form

Pickup costs a vehicle, a driver and an hour for what may be one carrier bag. The form must make every trip worth making.

### Fields

- Name and mobile number.
- Address with PIN code, landmark and floor.
- Item categories from your accepted list, with quantities in units people can estimate: bags, cartons, kilograms, pieces.
- One to three photographs, compressed in the browser before upload.
- Preferred slots.
- Consent to be contacted about this pickup, plus a separate, unticked option for future updates.

### Area, minimum quantity and slots

- **Serviceable area.** Check the PIN code as it is typed. Outside your area, show the nearest drop-off point at once.
- **Minimum quantity.** State the threshold ("five cartons or more, or one large item we have agreed to take"). Below it, offer drop-off or the next collection day.
- **Item rules.** Selecting something you do not accept shows the reason and removes it from the request.
- **Slots.** Offer real capacity: fixed windows on fixed days per zone, with a cap per window. The donor picks a window, staff confirm it, and the page says the request is pending until confirmed.

### OTP, uploads and spam

- Verify the mobile number with a one-time password before the request is created. This removes most fake and mistyped requests.
- Accept only images, check file type on the server, limit size, rename files and store them outside the public web folder.
- Add a honeypot field and rate limits, and cap open requests per phone number.

## Corporate and bulk offers

Companies, schools, housing societies and wholesalers need a separate form: organisation and contact person; what is offered, quantity, batch and expiry dates for packaged goods; where the goods are and who transports them; what documentation they expect; and whether any part comes from outside India.

**CSR.** Companies sometimes ask an NGO to certify donated goods as CSR spend. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs' CSR FAQs, issued with General Circular No. 14/2021 dated 25 August 2021, answer the question "whether contribution in kind can be monetized to be shown as CSR expenditure" with a no, reasoning from the requirement in section 135(5) of the Companies Act that the company spends the amount. Your page should say that you acknowledge goods as goods and do not certify them as CSR expenditure. Check the current MCA position before quoting it.

**Foreign source.** The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 defines foreign contribution to include the donation, delivery or transfer by a foreign source of any article, other than an article given to a person as a gift for personal use within a specified market value, which commentary on the rules gives as ₹1,00,000. Goods are not outside FCRA merely because no money moves. Route any offer from a foreign company, charity or other foreign source to the person responsible for FCRA compliance before anyone says yes. TODO (verify): confirm on the MHA FCRA portal or with your FCRA adviser how articles received in kind are recorded and reported; we could not open the official FAQ when writing.

## The staff side: workflow and inventory log

Each offer should become a record with a status and an owner:

1. **New:** received, number verified.
2. **Reviewed:** accepted, partly accepted or declined with a reason code (condition, not needed now, outside area, below minimum).
3. **Scheduled:** slot confirmed and assigned, visible on a day-wise route list.
4. **Received:** items counted at the door; the actual count often differs from the offer.
5. **Sorted:** usable items entered into stock; unusable items recorded with what was done with them.
6. **Acknowledged and closed.**

The inventory log need not be a warehouse system. Stock in by date, donor and category; stock out by date and programme; a running balance; and a disposal entry are enough for most NGOs. That balance drives the wish list. Decide with your accountant how donated goods are reflected in your books.

Drivers should see only the day's addresses. In-kind donors belong in your donor database with an in-kind history, so the same person is not a stranger when they later give money.

## Acknowledgement letters versus 80G receipts

### What the law says

Explanation 5 to section 80G of the Income-tax Act, 1961 states that no deduction shall be allowed under the section in respect of any donation unless the donation is of a sum of money. The Income-tax Act, 2025, which applies from 1 April 2026, carries the rule into section 133, where sub-section (4) reads: "The deduction under this section shall be allowed only for donation made as a sum of money." The position is unchanged: goods do not qualify for the donation deduction. Confirm any specific case with your chartered accountant.

### What that means for the website

- **No 80G-style receipt for goods.** The receipt template and numbering series used for money should be technically unavailable to in-kind records, not merely discouraged.
- **An acknowledgement of goods received instead**, with your organisation's name and registration details, a number from its own series, the date, the donor's name, the items and quantities actually received, and a sentence stating that it is not a receipt for income-tax deduction.
- **No rupee value estimated by the NGO.** You usually cannot verify what the goods are worth. If a donor wants a figure recorded, show it as "value as declared by the donor". Never inflate or estimate on a donor's behalf.
- **Say it before the donor gives.** One line under the form: "We acknowledge every donation of goods in writing. Donations of goods do not qualify for a tax deduction, so we cannot issue an 80G receipt for them."

A donor who wants a deduction can give money. Our article on [offline donations by bank transfer, cheque and cash](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-offline-donations-bank-transfer-cheque-cash-pledges-2026) explains how those gifts are recorded and receipted.

## Donor data, addresses and consent

A pickup form collects a home address, a phone number and photographs. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is built on notice and consent, and the DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025 with staged commencement; the rules on notice, safeguards and erasure are reported to take effect on 13 May 2027. Build to that standard now:

- a short notice at the form: what you collect, why, who sees it, and how to withdraw or complain;
- separate, unticked consent for future messages;
- scheduled deletion of pickup photographs and exact addresses a fixed period after closure, while the acknowledgement record is kept as long as your auditors require;
- no advertising or remarketing tags on the form pages.

Ask your legal adviser how the Act and Rules apply to you.

## Showing impact without overclaiming

- Report what you counted: "1,240 kg of dry rations received and issued to the kitchen, April to September." Do not convert kilograms into meals without a stated method.
- Do not publish a rupee total for goods received.
- Say what could not be used and where it went.
- Photograph storerooms and sorting tables, not beneficiaries, unless you hold consent for that use.

## Seasonal and emergency drives

Woollens before winter and school kits before June can run as dated campaigns on the same system: a drive page with its own short wish list, start and end dates, collection points and a target in units. After the end date the page switches to a closing note with totals.

After a flood, unsorted clothing arrives by the truckload while the real need is a few specific items or money. Prepare an emergency mode in advance: one switch that shows exactly what is needed, what is not, where to deliver, and that pickups are suspended. The guide to an [emergency and disaster relief appeal page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-emergency-disaster-relief-appeal-page-2026) covers the fundraising side, and the [volunteer sign-up page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-volunteer-signup-page-form-consent-follow-up-2026) guide covers recruiting people to sort and carry.

## WhatsApp confirmations that reduce calls

Four messages cover the journey: request received with a number; pickup confirmed with day and window, or declined with the reason and the drop-off alternative; a reminder the evening before; and a thank-you with the acknowledgement attached. Send them as approved utility templates through the [WhatsApp Business API](/whatsapp/business-api), from a number in your organisation's name, to people who opted in on the form. Keep addresses out of the message text. Do not run pickups from a staff member's personal WhatsApp, where addresses stay on a private handset.

## Build options for NGO website development in India: costs and timelines

These are indicative ranges for planning, not quotations. Languages, the number of centres and the state of the existing site move them either way.

| Option | What you get | Indicative cost | Indicative timeline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Page plus simple form | Accepted and not-accepted lists, drop-off points with map, wish list edited as page content, a form that emails staff | ₹15,000 to ₹40,000 added to an existing site | 1 to 2 weeks |
| 2. Structured module | Editable wish list and drop-off entries, pickup form with PIN-code and quantity rules, OTP, photo upload, status workflow, acknowledgement PDF, WhatsApp confirmations | ₹60,000 to ₹1,50,000 | 3 to 6 weeks |
| 3. Custom in-kind system | Option 2 plus multi-centre stock in and out, slot capacity and route lists, corporate offer pipeline, CRM link, drive pages, reports | ₹2,00,000 to ₹5,00,000 or more | 2 to 3 months |

**Included:** page design, the forms and rules described, admin screens, the acknowledgement template, phone testing and staff training.

**Not included:** your acceptance policy (you must decide it), photography, WhatsApp and SMS message charges, vehicles and people for pickups, and accounting or legal advice.

For options 2 and 3, budget an indicative ₹15,000 to ₹60,000 a year above existing website maintenance for support and messaging, and check it against real volumes after the first quarter. Most calendar time goes into decisions: what you accept, the pickup area and minimum, and who reviews requests. The [NGO website pricing](/pricing/ngo-website) page shows how the module fits into a full build.

## A worked example

This is an illustration, not a client case; the numbers are invented to show the mechanics.

A Pune trust runs a home for sixty children and a weekend community kitchen, with one office coordinator. It builds option 2.

- **Page.** Accepted: sealed dry rations, new stationery, washed children's clothes, working fans. Not accepted: medicines, mattresses, soft toys, adult clothing. Cooked food by arrangement through a separate short form.
- **Wish list.** Eighteen items, edited by the warden on her phone each Monday.
- **Pickup.** Twelve PIN codes, five cartons or more, Tuesday and Saturday mornings, at most six pickups a morning. Other requests are shown the drop-off address and hours.
- **Workflow.** The coordinator reviews requests each afternoon, declines two on condition after seeing the photographs, and confirms the rest.
- **Acknowledgement.** Each donor receives a WhatsApp message with a PDF listing what was received, numbered in an in-kind series, stating that it is not a tax-deduction receipt and showing no rupee value.

The trust still answers the phone, but most callers have read the page first.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Promising or implying an 80G receipt for goods.
- Putting the NGO's own rupee estimate on an acknowledgement.
- A wish list with no date, or one only a developer can change.
- Offering pickup everywhere, for any quantity.
- Taking a foreign-source or corporate bulk consignment through the household form.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can an NGO give an 80G receipt for donated clothes, food or other goods?

No. Explanation 5 to section 80G of the Income-tax Act, 1961 allows the deduction only for a donation of a sum of money, and section 133(4) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 keeps the same rule. An NGO can issue a written acknowledgement of the goods received, which should state that it is not a tax-deduction receipt.

### What should an in-kind donation acknowledgement letter include?

The NGO's name and registration details, an acknowledgement number and date, the donor's name, and a description and quantity of the items actually received. It should not carry a rupee value estimated by the NGO, and it should say that it is not a receipt for income-tax deduction.

### How do I add a donation wish list to an NGO website?

Build the wish list as an editable content type in the CMS, with fields for item, specification, category, urgency, programme and a visible or hidden switch. Let whoever manages the storeroom edit it, and show a "last updated" date automatically.

### Should an NGO offer free pickup for donated items?

Only within limits it can sustain. Set a serviceable area by PIN code, a minimum quantity and fixed pickup windows with a cap, and ask for photographs before confirming. Requests outside the rules should be shown drop-off points and hours instead.

### How much does it cost to add an in-kind donations page to an NGO website in India?

As an indicative range, a content page with a simple form costs about ₹15,000 to ₹40,000 added to an existing site. A structured module with an editable wish list, rule-based pickup form, workflow and WhatsApp confirmations costs about ₹60,000 to ₹1,50,000, and a custom multi-centre system starts at about ₹2,00,000.
